title: Pascal's night of fire (1654)
hook: a mathematician has an experience one night and writes Fire, sewing the note into his coat

segments.voice: Yesterday, the burden rolled away at the cross in Bunyan's dream. Your line was the burden rolled away. Did you let your shoulders drop, and set something down? Day eight hundred ninety.

After Blaise Pascal dies, a servant going through his clothes feels something stiff in the lining of his coat. Tucked inside, the story goes, is a folded piece of parchment, and inside that, a scrap of paper, both in Pascal's handwriting. He had sewn it in, and he is said to have moved it from coat to coat, without ever mentioning it to anyone. Pascal was a mathematician and inventor, a man of numbers and proofs. But the note in his coat isn't a proof. It's barely sentences. Near the top, one word. Today: Pascal's night of fire.

The word is Fire. The note itself gives the hours: from about half past ten at night until about half past midnight. Whatever happened, Pascal didn't try to explain it. He wrote in bursts, like someone catching his breath. Right after Fire, he writes, in effect: the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob, not of the philosophers and scholars. That's striking from a man who was a philosopher and a scholar. He isn't throwing away his mind. He's saying that what met him that night wasn't an idea he'd reasoned his way to. It was the God of a family story, the God who calls people by name. Those three names come straight from scripture. In Exodus, Moses sees a bush on fire that doesn't burn up. In the King James words, "the bush burned with fire, and the bush was not consumed." And the voice from the fire says, "I am the God of thy father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob." Pascal's night echoes that scene: a fire, and a God who is known by the people he has met. Further down, Pascal reaches for more words: certainty, feeling, joy, peace. Joy, he writes, again and again, and tears of joy. Then he sews it into his coat. Not to show anyone. To keep it close. Some readers see the note as the hidden center of everything Pascal wrote afterward. Nobody can say exactly what he saw. He gave us one word for it, and kept it against his chest.

Here's the practice: find one word for your deepest experience. Think of a moment in your life that you've never quite been able to explain, a moment of awe, of love, of being met, of clarity. Don't tell the whole story. Let it come back to you in the quiet, and wait for one word to rise for it. Just one, the way Pascal had Fire. If you pray, you can hold that moment before God. If you don't, simply hold it, and let the word arrive. The bell holds the time.
Pascal's night of fire. A mathematician's experience in the night, which he wrote down under the word Fire and kept sewn into his coat.
Your line: fire. Today, write your one word somewhere only you will see it, inside a wallet, on the back of a photo, in a pocket, and keep it close. Day eight hundred ninety.

howItsDone: Pascal's note, often called the Memorial, is read by Christians of different churches as a witness to a personal encounter with God, and some keep a copy of it or a short line from scripture close by in a similar way.

fork.setup: you're a mathematician. something happened to you one night that you can't explain. what do you do with it?
options: write it down in a few words and keep it close.
fork.reveal: Pascal wrote a short, broken note headed Fire, sewed it into his coat, and, the story goes, never mentioned it to anyone.

trapdoor: what you thought: a famous thinker had a mystical moment.
what it means: Pascal headed his note on two hours in the night with one word, Fire, and kept it sewn into his coat.
what a scholar hears: right after Fire, he names the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the words from the burning bush, not the god of philosophers.

notes: The Memorial is paraphrased, not quoted: I'm not certain of a public-domain English wording (Trotter 1910 may include it; if so, a Keeper could swap in exact words).
The hours (about half past ten to about half past twelve) are given in the Memorial itself; confirm wording. The index hook's 'two-hour' matches.
Discovery details to confirm: found by a servant after his death; parchment copy with the paper original inside; sewn into the lining; 'the story goes' he moved it from coat to coat.
The year 1654 is in the index title only; the voice gives no year (the Memorial itself is dated, so it could be added if the Keeper wishes).
'Pascal was a mathematician and inventor': general history; confirm wording.

Editor: cut the manuscript claim 'in large letters'; put the discovery details (parchment, paper, moving it coat to coat, never mentioning it) under 'the story goes' / 'is said to'; fixed a garbled sequence where 'those names come straight from scripture' followed the list of feeling words instead of the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.

Second editor pass: the myth answer and fork reveal no longer state as fact that he never mentioned the note (now 'is said' / 'the story goes', matching the hook); fixed the trapdoor line that read as if he spent two hours writing one word.
